title: Germs You Cannot See
bigQuestion: If germs are too small to see, how do we know where they are and how do we stop them?

story.title: The Glitter Hands
story.kicker: One sprinkle of glitter shows the whole class where hands have been.
paragraphs: Mr. Lopez put a spoon of glitter in Maya's hand. He asked her to rub her hands together. Then he said, "Go on with your morning. Do not wash yet." Maya opened the door. She picked a book. She sharpened a pencil. She gave Sam a high five.

At snack time the class looked around. There was glitter on the door handle. There was glitter on the pencil sharpener. There was glitter on the book. Sam had glitter on his hand. Sam had rubbed his nose. Now his nose sparkled.

"Glitter is easy to see," said Mr. Lopez. "Germs are not. But germs travel the same way. They ride on hands. They land on what we touch." Maya looked at her sparkly fingers. She thought about her snack.
Then Maya washed with soap and warm water. She scrubbed for twenty seconds. The glitter went down the drain. Her hands were clean. "That," said Mr. Lopez, "is what soap does to germs too."
story.think: Where did Maya's glitter travel? Where do you think germs travel in our classroom?

lessons.title: What a Germ Is
lessons.mainIdea: Germs are tiny living things that can make you sick, and they are too small to see.
reading: Look at your hand. It looks clean. But tiny *germs* may be on it right now. A germ is so small that a thousand could sit on the dot of this i. You cannot see them without a special tool called a microscope.
Some germs make people sick. They can give you a cold. They can give you a tummy ache. Germs get inside your body through your mouth, your nose and your eyes.
Clean hands keep germs out. That is why we wash. Washing is a job you can do all by yourself.

words.d: a tiny living thing, too small to see, that can make you sick
a tool that makes tiny things look big enough to see

look.title: The Dot on the i
look.text: Look at the dot on the letter i in the word 'sick'. Now picture a thousand tiny germs sitting on that dot. They are so small that the dot still looks the same. Now picture your whole hand.
look.prompt: If a thousand germs fit on one dot, how many could fit on your hand? Why can you not see them?

check.q: Why can't you see a germ on your hand?
choices: Germs are too small to see
Germs are the same color as skin
Germs only come out at night
check.why: Germs are so tiny that you need a microscope to see them.

check.q: Which tool lets people see germs?
check.why: A microscope makes tiny things look big enough to see.

check.q: How do germs get inside your body?
choices: Through your mouth, nose and eyes
check.why: Germs enter through the mouth, nose and eyes, so clean hands matter before you touch your face.

lessons.title: Germs Ride on Hands
lessons.mainIdea: Germs travel on hands, in coughs and sneezes, and on food.
reading: Germs cannot walk. They cannot fly on their own. They need a ride. Hands are their favorite ride. You touch a door handle. Germs hop on. You touch your mouth. Germs hop off, right inside you.
A cough or a sneeze is a ride too. Tiny drops fly out of your mouth. Germs ride the drops. They land on desks, toys and other people.
Food can carry germs too. If dirty hands touch a sandwich, the germs go on the sandwich. Then you eat them. Clean hands keep food clean.

words.d: to move from one place or person to another

look.title: Follow the Germ
look.text: Ben sneezes into his hand. He does not wash. He picks up the red crayon. Ava uses the red crayon next. Then Ava eats a cracker with that hand. Follow the germ from Ben's sneeze to Ava's cracker.
look.prompt: Name each stop the germ made. Where could someone have stopped it?

check.q: What is a germ's favorite way to travel?
check.why: Germs ride on hands from the things we touch to our mouths.

check.q: Ben sneezes into his hand and picks up a crayon. What happened?
choices: Germs moved from his hand to the crayon
check.why: Germs spread from a dirty hand to anything it touches.

check.q: Dirty hands touch a sandwich. Where do the germs go?
choices: They go back to the door
check.why: Germs on hands move onto food, and then into the person who eats it.

lessons.title: Before You Eat
lessons.mainIdea: Always wash your hands before you eat or touch food.
reading: It is lunch time. Your hands have touched a lot today. The bus rail. Your desk. The ball at recess. Now you will pick up a sandwich with those hands. Stop. Wash first.
Wash before every meal and every snack. Wash before you help make food too. Germs from your hands can go on the food. Then they go in your mouth.
Make it a habit. Line up. Wash. Then sit down to eat. Your food stays clean, and so do you.

words.d: something you do the same way every time without having to think about it

look.title: The Lunch Line
look.text: Picture the lunch line. Kai has his tray. He just came in from recess. He touched the swing, the slide and the door. He has not washed. His hands are about to touch his apple.
look.prompt: What should Kai do before he picks up the apple? What might happen if he does not?

check.q: When should you wash before lunch?
choices: Only if your hands look dirty
check.why: Germs you cannot see can be on your hands, so wash before every meal and snack.

check.q: Kai came in from recess. What is the first step before eating?
check.why: Recess hands touched many things; washing with soap takes the germs off.

check.q: Why wash before helping make food?
choices: So germs do not get on the food
check.why: Hands that touch food can put germs on it, so clean hands keep food clean.

lessons.title: After the Bathroom and Outside
lessons.mainIdea: Wash after using the bathroom and after playing outside.
reading: The bathroom is full of germs you cannot see. They are on the handle. They are on the seat. After you use the bathroom, wash your hands. Every time. Even if you are in a hurry.
Outside is fun and a little dirty. Dirt, bugs and playground bars all carry germs. When you come inside, go to the sink. Wash before you do anything else.
Here is the rule. Bathroom, then wash. Outside, then wash. No skipping, even when you are in a hurry.

words.d: something you always do the same way to stay safe

look.title: Wash Times in One Day
look.prompt: Add up the times. How many washes is that in one day? Which one happens the most?

check.q: You just used the bathroom. What do you do next?
check.why: Bathroom germs are on hands and handles, so wash every single time.

check.q: You come in from the playground. What comes first?
check.why: Playground bars and dirt carry germs, so wash before anything else.

check.q: In the data, which wash happened the most?
check.why: The table shows 3 washes after the bathroom, more than any other row.

lessons.title: After Pets and Sneezes
lessons.mainIdea: Wash after you touch a pet and after you cough or sneeze.
reading: You pet a dog. The dog is soft and happy. But the dog's fur has germs. So does its mouth. After you touch any pet, wash your hands. Wash after feeding a pet too.
You sneeze. Drops fly out. Some land on your hand. If you touch a toy now, the germs go on the toy. So wash after you sneeze or cough. Wash after you blow your nose.
Pets, sneezes, tissues. All three mean go wash. Say it to yourself. Pets, sneezes, tissues, wash.

words.d: a soft paper you use to blow your nose, then throw away

look.title: Three Kids, Three Reasons
look.text: Lena just fed the class hamster. Omar just blew his nose. Rosa just petted the neighbor's cat. All three walk to the reading rug. None of them stopped at the sink.
look.prompt: Which of the three should wash? Why did each one need to?

check.q: You just petted a dog. What should you do?
choices: Rub your hands on your pants
check.why: Pet fur and mouths carry germs, so wash after touching any animal.

check.q: You blow your nose with a tissue. Then what?
choices: Put the tissue in your pocket
Throw it away and wash your hands
Hand the tissue to a friend
check.why: The tissue and your hands both have germs; toss the tissue and wash.

check.q: Which one does NOT need a wash right after?
check.why: Reading does not put new germs on your hands; pets and sneezes do.

lessons.title: Soap Lifts, Water Carries
lessons.mainIdea: Soap lifts germs off your skin, and running water carries them down the drain.
reading: Germs stick to skin. Water alone slides right past them. That is why you need *soap*. Soap grabs germs and dirt. It lifts them up off your skin.
Then water does its job. Running water carries the loose germs away. Down the drain they go. Soap and water are a team.
Try it. Wet your hands. Add soap. Rub until you see bubbles. Rinse. Feel how clean your hands are.

words.d: what lifts germs and dirt off your skin so water can wash them away
to run clean water over something to wash the soap away

look.title: Two Sinks
look.text: At sink one, Jada rinses her hands with water only. She counts to three. At sink two, Theo wets his hands, rubs on soap, scrubs until bubbles cover his hands, and then rinses.
look.prompt: Whose hands are cleaner? What did soap do that water alone could not?

check.q: What does soap do?
check.why: Soap grabs germs and dirt and lifts them off so water can carry them away.

check.q: Jada used water only for three seconds. What is wrong?
choices: No soap, so the germs stayed stuck
check.why: Water alone slides past germs; soap is needed to lift them.

check.q: What carries the loose germs away?
check.why: After soap lifts the germs, rinsing under running water washes them down the drain.

lessons.title: Cough Into Your Elbow
lessons.mainIdea: Cover a cough or sneeze with your elbow, not your hand.
reading: A cough is coming. Where does it go? Not into the air. Not into your hand. Into your *elbow*. Bend your arm. Put your mouth in the crook. Cough there.
Why the elbow? Your elbow does not touch door handles. It does not pick up crayons. Your hand does. Germs in your elbow stay put.
If you use a tissue, throw it away right away. Then wash your hands with soap. Cover, toss, wash.

words.d: the bend in the middle of your arm

look.title: Where the Sneeze Went
look.text: Picture Nia feeling a sneeze. She bends her arm and sneezes into her elbow. Next to her, Leo sneezes into his open hand. Then Leo picks up the class tablet. Nia picks up her pencil with a clean hand.
look.prompt: Who spread germs to something the class shares? What should Leo do now?

check.q: Where should a cough go?
check.why: The elbow does not touch shared things, so germs stay put.

check.q: Leo sneezed into his hand and grabbed the tablet. What happened?
check.why: Hands touch shared things; germs on the hand moved to the tablet.

check.q: You used a tissue for a sneeze. What is the last step?
choices: Put the tissue on the desk
check.why: Cover, toss, wash: the tissue goes in the trash and hands get washed.

review.q: Why can you not see germs on your hands?
choices: They only live in the bathroom
review.why: Germs are so tiny they need a microscope to be seen.

review.q: How do germs get from a door handle into your body?
choices: Your hand touches the handle, then your mouth
review.why: Germs ride on hands from things we touch to our mouth, nose and eyes.

review.q: Which is a time to wash your hands?
review.why: Bathroom handles and seats carry germs, so wash every time after.

review.q: What does soap do that water alone cannot?
choices: Makes your hands smell like flowers
review.why: Soap grabs germs so running water can carry them away.

review.q: A cough is coming. Where does it go?
review.why: The elbow does not touch shared things, so germs stay put.

review.q: In the glitter story, what did the glitter stand for?
review.why: Glitter showed where hands had been, just like germs travel on hands.
